title: From skill to paid work: discovery, pricing and reporting
course_title: Search Engine Optimization (SEO): Professional Audits and Client Practice

say: From skill to paid work: discovery, pricing and reporting.
This is the video for module three of the professional SEO course.
Discovery is where SEO projects succeed or fail. If you do not know which enquiries make the client money, you will optimise the wrong pages.

panel.heading: Turn technical skill into trusted work

Write a report an owner reads in minutes

say: In this video you will learn to ask the right questions, get safe access, price your work clearly, and report in plain language.

say: First, goals. What does a good month look like, and how do enquiries arrive? By form, phone, WhatsApp or walk-in?

panel.heading: Five areas every call covers
items: Goals: which products or services bring profit
Customers: the words they actually use
History: past SEO, redesigns, domain moves
Competitors they really lose jobs to
Constraints: budget, developer time, deadlines

say: Second, customers. Ask for five recent enquiries, with personal details removed, and note their words.

say: Third, history. For example, Blessing's logistics firm in Port Harcourt moved to a new domain and nobody set up redirects. That became the first thing to investigate.

say: Then competitors, checked with your own phone search, and constraints. Send a one-page brief within two working days, and ask the client to confirm it in writing.

say: Owners can add you with your own Google account. For most audits, ask for full user. Ownership stays with the client, so they never lose control if you stop working together.

panel.heading: Getting access the safe way
left: Ask for full user in Search Console
Viewer or Analyst role in GA4
A named website account for you
Remove your access at the end
right: Become the owner of their property
Keep customer data after the project

say: Never ask for a password. Data can include names and phone numbers, and the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 governs it. Request only what you need, protect it with two-step verification, and delete copies when the project ends.

say: There is no official rate, so research your market. Ngozi chose an illustrative rate of 10,000 naira an hour. She adds up her audit tasks: 20 hours.

card.title: Ngozi prices an audit and a retainer
card.note: Illustrative rate. Naira prices are approximate.

say: 20 hours times 10,000 is 200,000 naira.

card.title: Ngozi prices an audit and a retainer
card.note: Illustrative rate. Naira prices are approximate.

say: She adds 15% contingency for surprises, like a messy domain history. That makes 230,000 naira.

card.title: Ngozi prices an audit and a retainer
card.note: Illustrative rate. Naira prices are approximate.

say: To implement the plan, she offers a retainer of 16 hours a month, 160,000 naira, with a 3-month minimum of 480,000 naira. She asks for 50% before work starts and 50% on delivery.
Every number traces back to hours and a rate, so if the client wants a discount, she can reduce scope instead of just cutting the price.

say: Scope creep arrives politely. The bookshop owner asks Ngozi to also review 15 blog posts. She answers warmly, in writing, and says it is outside the agreed scope.

panel.heading: When the client asks for extra

Record the decision

say: She estimates about 4 hours, which is 40,000 naira at the agreed rate.

say: She offers to add it now, swap it for something in the current scope, or leave it for later. The owner chooses later, and Ngozi records the decision.

say: In every proposal, never promise positions, and never include bought links or automated content. Google's spam policies prohibit them, and the client's site carries the risk.

panel.rule: No ranking promises. No bought links. No mass-produced pages.

say: An owner reads for three things: what is wrong, what it costs, and what happens next. So lead with a one-page summary he can read on his phone.
Remove the jargon, but keep the numbers. Say your main service pages take almost five seconds to show on a phone, not mobile LCP is poor.

panel.heading: A report an owner understands fast
items: One-page summary first
Findings in priority order
Roadmap: days 1 to 30, 31 to 60, 61 to 90
Measurement plan from the brief
Technical appendix for the developer

say: Zainab targets logistics firms in Rivers State. She plans to contact 80 businesses, each with a personal note naming one issue she saw on their site.
Never send bulk unsolicited messages or add people to WhatsApp groups without consent.

panel.heading: Zainab's 90-day outreach plan
items: Contact 80 firms with a personal note
Assume 15% reply: 12 replies
Half book a call: 6 discovery calls
One in three accepts: 2 new clients
Week 8: compare real numbers and adjust

say: Using her own planning assumptions, 15% reply, half of those book a call, and one in three accepts. That is 2 new clients.

say: To remember. Confirm a written brief before you price. Keep ownership with the client. Price from hours and a rate. Handle extras with a written change request. And report in plain language, with case studies shared only with permission.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Cover all five discovery areas, then confirm a brief
Full user access; ownership stays with the client
Price from hours x rate plus contingency
Extra requests: add, swap or defer, in writing
Plain language, real numbers, honest case studies

say: Now practise with a real small business. Run a discovery call, send a brief, price your audit, write your summary and plan your outreach.
Continue with the lessons below.
